lessons.title: College vs NBA rules
lessons.objective: Explain the key rule differences between college and NBA basketball.

payload.prompt: How long is a college men's basketball game?

options.text: Two 20-minute halves, 40 minutes total.
Four 12-minute quarters, 48 minutes total (like the NBA).
Four 10-minute quarters, 40 minutes total (like women's college).

explanation.correct: Right. College men play two halves of 20 minutes each. Women play four 10-minute quarters.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. College men play two 20-minute halves, different from both the NBA and women's college.

payload.prompt: When do players foul out in college basketball?

options.text: After five personal fouls (NBA and WNBA allow six).
After six personal fouls like the NBA.
After three fouls in the first half, four in the second.

explanation.correct: Right. College players foul out at five; the NBA and WNBA allow six fouls.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. College is five fouls for disqualification, one fewer than the NBA.

payload.prompt: Match college basketball rules to their key differences from the NBA.

pairs.definition: 30 seconds in college (24 in the NBA and WNBA).
Fully legal in college; the NBA adds a defensive three-second rule that limits camping in the lane.
22 feet 1.75 inches in college, shorter than the NBA's 23 feet 9 inches at the top.

distractorDefinitions: Men's college uses a smaller ball than the NBA.
College games have no shot clock at all.

explanation.summary: College has a 30-second shot clock, allows any zone, and draws its three-point line closer to the rim than the NBA does. The men's ball is the same size.

payload.prompt: A college player with four fouls stays in the game. True?

choices.label: Yes, can play until the fifth.

explanation.correct: Right. In college, players can have up to five fouls before fouling out. A fourth foul does not end their night.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. College allows five fouls. The fourth foul does not disqualify the player.

statement.speaker: Your crush
statement.text: Ugh, they are in the bonus already. Seven fouls in a half and we are shooting free throws.

payload.question: What is she saying?

options.text: A college team's fouls add up across a whole half, and the bonus starts at seven.
College teams get the bonus on the fifth foul of every quarter.
There is no bonus in college basketball.
The bonus means the other team gets the ball back.

payload.translation: She means a college team's fouls are counted over a 20-minute half. From the seventh, the other team shoots a one-and-one, and from the tenth, two free throws. The NBA counts per quarter instead.

followUps.line: So the count resets at halftime?
followUps.why: A curious question that checks the halves idea without pretending to know the details.

followUps.line: That sounds different from the NBA. Is it easier to get in the bonus?
followUps.why: Shows you noticed the difference and lets her explain.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Halves change the foul math. If you are unsure of the exact numbers, ask her what she is seeing.

lessons.title: March Madness: how the bracket works
lessons.objective: Explain the NCAA tournament structure, seeding and the upset magic.

payload.prompt: How many teams make the NCAA men's basketball tournament?

options.text: 68 teams: 64 in the main bracket plus four in the First Four.
64 teams in a simple single-elimination bracket.
32 teams in a bracket with no play-in games.

explanation.correct: Right. 68 teams make the NCAA tournament. The First Four is four play-in games for the last at-large teams and the lowest-seeded automatic qualifiers.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. The NCAA tournament has 68 teams: 64 in the main bracket and four in First Four play-in games.

payload.prompt: What is Selection Sunday?

options.text: The day the NCAA announces the 68-team tournament bracket and seeding.
A TV show where fans vote on tournament teams.
The first day of the tournament games.

explanation.correct: Right. Selection Sunday is when the NCAA tournament bracket is revealed and teams learn their seeds and first-round opponents.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. Selection Sunday is the official selection and seeding of the 68 NCAA tournament teams.

payload.prompt: Order the NCAA tournament timeline from earliest to latest.

items.text: College basketball regular season and conference tournaments
Selection Sunday: NCAA announces the 68-team bracket

explanation.correct: Right. Conference tournaments end on the weekend before Selection Sunday, then the First Four trims the field to 64 and the bracket plays down to the Final Four in April.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. The order is the regular season and conference tournaments, Selection Sunday, the First Four, the first round of 64 and then the Final Four in April.

statement.speaker: Your crush
statement.text: My team got stuck in the First Four. We have to win a game just to get a real first round.

payload.question: What is she annoyed about?

options.text: Her team has to win a play-in game before it even reaches the 64-team bracket.
Her team was left out of the tournament entirely.
The First Four is played after the Final Four.
Her team has to play four games in one day.

payload.translation: She means her team is one of the last teams in the field, so it plays a First Four game first. Win it and it joins the round of 64, and First Four teams have gone on deep runs before.

followUps.line: Who do you get if you win it?
followUps.why: A curious question that keeps you in her world and lets her explain the bracket.

followUps.line: Doesn't a win there get you on a roll, though?
followUps.why: A gentle, optimistic angle: some First Four winners have gone on deep runs.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Being in the First Four is annoying, but it still means being in the tournament. Ask how she feels about it.

statement.speaker: Your crush
statement.text: A 14 seed just knocked out my three seed. My bracket is dead.

payload.question: What is she expressing?

options.text: A big first-round upset (14 seed over a 3 seed) broke her predictions early.
Her three seed is breaking apart as a program.
Basketball is literally dying.
The 14 seed is playing unfairly.

payload.translation: She is frustrated that an upset unraveled her bracket predictions early. March Madness is known for surprises.

followUps.line: Do upsets make it more fun to watch even if your picks are wrong?
followUps.why: Gentle reframe that shows the appeal of bracket chaos.

followUps.line: How many games did you get right so far?
followUps.why: Shifts to what she got right instead of dwelling on the loss.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Bracket busting is part of the March Madness charm. Acknowledge her loss and ask what made the upset surprising.

lessons.title: Getting in: NET, quad wins and the bubble
lessons.objective: Explain how college teams earn their NCAA tournament bid and what metrics matter.

payload.prompt: What is the NET ranking in college basketball?

options.text: NCAA Evaluation Tool: a ranking system the NCAA uses to help select and seed tournament teams.
A metric that measures how many games a team has to win.
The final bracket seeding determined by fans.

explanation.correct: Right. The NET is the NCAA's evaluation tool, ranking all Division I teams by performance and strength of schedule.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. The NET is the NCAA Evaluation Tool, used for tournament selection and seeding.

payload.prompt: What are quad wins in college basketball?

options.text: Wins categorized by opponent strength: Quad 1 is best teams, Quad 4 is the weakest.
Four consecutive wins in a row.
Wins that happen in the four quarters of a game.

explanation.correct: Right. Quad wins rank opponents by quality. Quad 1 wins (against top-ranked teams) matter most for NCAA selection.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. Quad wins are categorized by opponent strength, with Quad 1 wins being the most valuable.

payload.prompt: Does this team deserve to make the NCAA tournament?

situation.narrative: Late in the season, a mid-major team is fighting for an NCAA tournament spot.

options.label: Yes, they are in the tournament.
options.consequence: You think the record and Quad 1 wins earn an at-large bid. That is possible, but a NET near 75 is not a lock, so calling them in is too confident.
considerations: Twenty-three wins and three Quad 1 wins are real resume items.
A NET near 75 is borderline, not a lock, for an at-large spot.
The weaker conference schedule might count against them.

options.label: No, they should be an NIT team.
options.consequence: You weigh the weak schedule and early conference-tournament exit heavily. That is reasonable, but it is too early to rule them out.
considerations: Teams from weaker conferences often sit on the bubble.
Losing early in the conference tournament meant no automatic bid.
A NET near 75 is borderline, not hopeless, for an at-large bid.

options.label: They are on the bubble; it depends on other results.
options.consequence: You understand that late-season results and other bubble teams' outcomes decide their fate. This is reality.
considerations: The tournament selection is relative; they are compared to other bubble teams.
Other teams' results in the final days shift bubble positions.
This team could be in or out by just a few wins from other bubble teams.

payload.expertNote: College tournament selection is subjective. The committee considers NET ranking, quad wins, strength of schedule, and recent results. Bubble teams often depend on how other bubble teams finish.

payload.prompt: What percentage of college basketball teams make the NCAA tournament?

explanation.correct: Right. 68 of roughly 360 Division I men's teams make the tournament, which is about one in five. Conference champions get in automatically, and the rest are at-large picks.
explanation.incorrect: The NCAA tournament takes 68 of roughly 360 Division I men's teams, about one in five. Conference champions get automatic bids and the committee picks the rest.

statement.speaker: Your crush
statement.text: Our team is on the bubble. We might not make it even though we won twenty games.

payload.question: What is she saying?

options.text: Her team is borderline for NCAA tournament selection; 20 wins is good but might not be enough.
Her team is definitely out of the tournament.
Twenty wins guarantees a tournament bid.
The tournament is held on a bubble.

payload.translation: She understands the bubble: 20 wins does not guarantee entry. It depends on the tournament field and other bubble teams.

followUps.line: What Quad wins do they have?
followUps.why: Good follow-up that shows you know quality wins matter more than total wins.

followUps.line: If they win out, are they in?
followUps.why: Asks if late-season momentum could seal their tournament spot.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: The bubble is real in college basketball. Acknowledge her anxiety; it is a stressful late-season reality.

lessons.title: Portal, NIL and the House settlement
lessons.objective: Explain the transfer portal, Name Image Likeness and revenue sharing in college basketball.

payload.prompt: What is the transfer portal in college basketball?

options.text: A system where players can declare their intent to transfer, making them available for other teams to recruit.
A website where only upperclassmen can play.
A rule that prevents any player from changing schools.

explanation.correct: Right. The transfer portal is how modern college players move between schools. It opened up the recruitment landscape dramatically.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. The transfer portal is a registration system for players entering the transfer market.

payload.prompt: Match college basketball policy changes to what they allow.

pairs.definition: Athletes can earn money from their own name, image and likeness, such as endorsements. It began in 2021.
Players enter their name and other schools can recruit them to transfer.
Since the House settlement, schools can pay athletes directly, under a cap of about $20 million per school.

distractorDefinitions: A rule that bans players from ever changing schools.
A requirement that every athlete sign a shoe deal.

explanation.summary: NIL lets athletes earn from their name, the portal makes changing schools easy, and revenue sharing lets schools pay athletes directly. Dollar caps change, so check the current figure.

statement.speaker: Your crush
statement.text: He just entered the portal. I hope another good school picks him up.

payload.question: What is she saying?

options.text: She is expressing hope that the player will transfer to another quality program.
She thinks he is leaving college permanently.
The portal is a literal physical location.
She wants him to drop out of school.

payload.translation: She means a player has put his name in the transfer portal, so other schools can now recruit him. She is hoping a strong program picks him up.

followUps.line: Why would a good program want him?
followUps.why: Good follow-up that explores what makes a portal player attractive.

followUps.line: Where do you want him to land?
followUps.why: A warm question that lets her share her favorite destinations.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: The transfer portal talk is common now. Acknowledge her hope for the player; it shows she cares about their career.

statement.speaker: Your crush
statement.text: NIL deals changed everything. Now players can actually make money in college.

payload.question: What is she acknowledging?

options.text: NIL lets college athletes earn money from their name and image, which they could not do before 2021.
College players now make NBA-level salaries.
All athletes are required to sign NIL deals.
NIL deals are only for elite athletes.

payload.translation: She means players can now sign endorsement and sponsorship deals, which changed how recruiting and roster-building work.

followUps.line: Does that change how you view college basketball?
followUps.why: Good follow-up that asks her perspective on amateurism vs professionalism.

followUps.line: Who gets the biggest NIL deals?
followUps.why: Asks what she knows about market value in college sports.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: People disagree about whether NIL is good for college sports. Ask her view instead of picking a side.

payload.prompt: A college player signs a sponsorship deal. Allowed today?

scene.alt: A college basketball player holding a sponsor's product.

explanation.correct: Yes. Since 2021, name, image and likeness rules let college athletes sign endorsements. Schools can now also pay players directly through revenue sharing.
explanation.incorrect: That was the old rule. Since 2021, NIL lets college athletes earn money from endorsements, and schools can now also pay players through revenue sharing.

lessons.title: Conferences, blue bloods and mid-majors
lessons.objective: Understand college basketball's conference structure and competitive hierarchy.

payload.prompt: What is a blue blood in college basketball?

options.text: A historic, elite program with many tournament appearances, championships and sustained success.
A team that only plays in blue jerseys.
A program that won the tournament only once.

explanation.correct: Right. Blue bloods are the elite programs: Duke, North Carolina, Kansas, UCLA, etc. They are known for sustained excellence.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. Blue bloods are the elite, traditionally successful college basketball programs.

payload.prompt: What is a mid-major college basketball program?

options.text: A strong program from outside the biggest conferences, usually with a smaller budget.
A program in its second year of Division I play.
Any program that is not in the NBA.

explanation.correct: Right. Mid-majors are solid programs from outside the biggest conferences, like Dayton or Florida Atlantic, which reached the 2023 Final Four. They often compete with smaller budgets.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. A mid-major is a competitive program from outside the biggest conferences. It is not about how long a school has played Division I.

payload.prompt: Match the college hoops labels.

pairs.definition: A historic elite program like Duke, North Carolina, Kansas or UCLA.
A strong program from outside the biggest conferences, like Dayton.
A low seed that makes an unexpected deep tournament run.

distractorDefinitions: A team that only plays early-morning games.
A program that has never made the tournament.

explanation.summary: Blue bloods are the traditional powers, mid-majors are strong programs outside the biggest conferences, and a Cinderella is whoever crashes the bracket as a long shot.

statement.speaker: Your crush
statement.text: I love when a mid-major makes a tournament run. It is the only way a Cinderella can happen.

payload.question: What is she appreciating?

options.text: She likes when smaller programs have unexpected success against elite teams.
She thinks only one team can make the tournament.
She dislikes blue-blood teams.
Cinderella is literally a college team.

payload.translation: She enjoys the underdog narrative. Mid-major Cinderella runs are part of March Madness appeal.

followUps.line: Do you remember a great Cinderella story?
followUps.why: Good follow-up that lets her share a favorite upset memory.

followUps.line: Is it harder for mid-majors to compete now with the portal?
followUps.why: Asks if she has thought about how transfers affect competitive balance.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Cinderella runs are a big part of why people love the tournament. Ask her favorite one.

payload.prompt: Can a mid-major reach the Final Four?

scene.alt: A tournament bracket with a low seed advancing to the Final Four.

explanation.correct: Yes. George Mason (2006), Butler (2010 and 2011), VCU (2011) and Florida Atlantic (2023) all got there from outside the big conferences. That is the Cinderella dream.
explanation.incorrect: It has happened several times: George Mason in 2006, Butler in 2010 and 2011, VCU in 2011 and Florida Atlantic in 2023. Mid-majors can go all the way to the Final Four.

lessons.title: Recruiting and coaching culture
lessons.objective: Explain how college coaches build rosters and why recruiting is the lifeblood of college basketball.

payload.prompt: What is a one-and-done player in college basketball?

options.text: A top recruit who plays one season in college then enters the NBA draft.
A player who only plays in one-point games.
A player who fouls out in every game.

explanation.correct: Right. One-and-done players spend a single season in college and then turn pro. The NBA's age rule is why top recruits often take that route, and many sign with blue bloods.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. One-and-done refers to top recruits playing one college season before the NBA draft.

payload.prompt: What does it mean when a recruit commits to a school?

options.text: He publicly announces he plans to play for that school.
He signs a pro contract with that school.
He has already played his first college game there.

explanation.correct: Right. A commitment is the public announcement of where a recruit plans to play. It is when fans start celebrating, even before the formal signing.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. A commitment is a recruit announcing where he plans to play, often months before he ever plays a game for the school.

payload.prompt: Her coach just left. What worries her most right now?

situation.narrative: A mid-major coach just took a bigger job in the coaching carousel. The transfer portal window opens soon, and the roster is full of players who could leave.

facts.label: Roster
facts.value: Several starters could enter the portal

facts.label: Timing
facts.value: Portal window opens in a few weeks

options.label: Who the new coach is, and whether the players stay
options.consequence: That is the real worry. In the portal era, a coaching change can empty a roster fast, so fans watch who is hired and who commits to stay.
considerations: Players can transfer freely when the coach leaves
A quick, credible hire helps keep the roster together
Recruits can reopen their commitments too

options.label: Who they will play in November
options.consequence: The schedule is months away. The roster and the new coach are the urgent questions.
considerations: Non-conference games do not matter until the team exists
The roster is the open question

options.label: Nothing, because the players are under contract
options.consequence: College players are not locked in. A coaching change is exactly when many enter the portal.
considerations: College players can transfer without sitting out
Commitments and scholarships do not work like pro contracts

payload.expertNote: The coaching carousel and the portal are linked. When a coach leaves, the roster and the incoming class can change quickly, so fans follow the hire and the commitments.

payload.title: Recruiting talk
payload.setting: She just mentioned her favorite recruit committed to her team. How do you respond?

exchanges.theirMessage: Yes! The top recruit just committed to us! He is going to change everything.

replies.text: That is awesome. What does he bring to the team?
replies.theirResponse: He is a scorer and a defender. We needed both.
replies.coachNote: Perfect. You matched her excitement and asked what makes him valuable. She felt heard.

replies.text: That is great. Does he need a year to adjust to college, or is he ready now?
replies.theirResponse: Good question. He is strong, so maybe day one.
replies.coachNote: Nice. You brought some nuance without raining on her parade. She appreciated the realistic angle.

replies.text: One recruit does not change much.
replies.coachNote: Ouch. You dismissed her joy. Next time celebrate with her even if you are skeptical about one recruit.

payload.closingNote: Recruiting talk is about hope and momentum. Share her excitement for the new talent; big recruits do move the needle.

statement.speaker: Your crush
statement.text: The coach built this team through the portal. Almost nobody is from the original recruiting class.

payload.question: What is she observing?

options.text: She is noting that the roster turned over via transfers, not through the original recruits.
The coach is not allowed to recruit.
The portal is a physical classroom.
Original recruits are always the best.

payload.translation: She means most of this roster arrived as transfers instead of freshman recruits, which is how many teams are built now.

followUps.line: Do portal teams gel faster or slower than built-in-house teams?
followUps.why: Good follow-up exploring chemistry and cohesion with portal players.

followUps.line: Is that why they feel so different this year?
followUps.why: A curious question that invites her to describe how the team has changed.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Portal-built rosters are common now. Ask her how this team feels different from the old recruiting-class teams.

lessons.title: Following {{team}} through the season
lessons.objective: Connect college basketball fandom to following your team from November through the tournament.

payload.prompt: When does college basketball conference play mostly begin?

options.text: Around New Year's, after a November and December of non-conference games.
On opening night in early November.
Right after Selection Sunday.

explanation.correct: Right. The season tips off in early November with non-conference games, then conference play mostly starts around New Year's and runs to early March.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. November and December are mostly non-conference games. Conference play mostly starts around New Year's, and Selection Sunday comes much later, in March.

payload.prompt: Fill in the blanks about the college basketball calendar.
payload.template: The season starts in {{start-month}}. Conference tournaments happen in {{conf-month}}, and the NCAA tournament begins in {{tourney-month}}.

explanation.correct: Right. The season starts in November, conference tournaments fill early March, and the NCAA tournament starts in mid-March and finishes in early April.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. The season starts in November, conference tournaments are in March, and the NCAA tournament starts in March and runs into April.

payload.prompt: How many college basketball games does a team play in a full season?

explanation.correct: Right. A typical team plays around 30 to 35 games: a dozen or so non-conference games, 18 to 20 conference games, and a conference tournament run. That is far fewer than the NBA's 82.
explanation.incorrect: A typical college team plays around 30 to 35 games: a dozen or so non-conference games, 18 to 20 conference games and some conference-tournament games. That is far fewer than the NBA's 82.

payload.title: {{team}} tournament talk
payload.setting: Selection Sunday is here and you are waiting to see your team's tournament seed and first opponent. How do you chat?

exchanges.theirMessage: I am so nervous. I hope we make it and get a good seed.

replies.text: Fingers crossed. Can we watch the reveal together?
replies.theirResponse: Yes please. I would love the company.
replies.coachNote: Warm and honest. You offered company instead of a prediction you cannot back up.

replies.text: What seed do you think we get if we make it?
replies.theirResponse: Maybe a 5 or 6 seed if we are lucky.
replies.coachNote: Perfect. You asked her prediction, which let her engage actively instead of just venting her anxiety.

replies.text: Do not worry, it does not matter. Everyone makes the tournament anyway.
replies.theirResponse: That is not true and you know it.
replies.coachNote: Ouch. You minimized her real stress. Next time acknowledge that Selection Sunday matters to fans.

payload.closingNote: Selection Sunday is a big deal for college fans. Share her anticipation and curiosity about the bracket.

statement.speaker: Your crush
statement.text: We made the tournament as a 12-seed! The matchup is tough but anything can happen in March.

payload.question: What is she expressing?

options.text: She is excited about making the tournament but realistic about the tough first-round matchup.
A 12-seed automatically loses in the first round.
March Madness never has surprises.
Seeds do not matter in college basketball.

payload.translation: She is balancing excitement with caution. A 12-seed is in the tournament but faces a tough draw. March Madness is indeed unpredictable.

followUps.line: Who is the 5-seed you are playing?
followUps.why: Good follow-up that shows you are paying attention to the bracket and matchup.

followUps.line: Does your team match up well against them?
followUps.why: Asks for her analysis, showing you value her basketball knowledge.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: 12 seeds beat 5 seeds often enough that fans call it the classic upset. Ask her who she would be most nervous about.
